text:
Help me write a public comment. I run a charter fishing boat out of our harbor, and the state fish and wildlife commission is taking comment on cutting the daily summer flounder limit from 4 fish per angler to 2.

Facts:
- I've run my boat for 22 years. I take out about 160 trips a season at $900 a trip for up to 6 people.
- There are 11 charter boats in our harbor.
- In a survey our charter association ran, 41 of 70 past customers said they would book fewer trips if the limit drops to 2. 12 said they'd book the same number.
- The commission staff's report says the flounder stock is at 78% of its target and recommends the cut for 3 years.
- Charter boats land about 9% of the state's summer flounder. Private boats land about 80%.
- The last time the limit was cut, in 2016, my bookings dropped from 170 trips to 138 the next season and came back to 155 two years later.

I want to say this limit will put every charter boat in our harbor out of business. I get two minutes at the microphone.

Before I draft, there's one problem with the main line, and I have a few questions.

**"Every charter boat in our harbor will go out of business" is more than your facts can carry, and your own history works against it.** In 2016 the limit was cut, you lost 32 trips (from 170 to 138, a 19% drop), and you stayed in business. Two years later you were back to 155. A commissioner who has heard "this will shut us down" at every hearing will stop listening there. You also only have figures for your own boat, not the other ten.

Your facts do support a strong claim, though:

- **What the last cut cost.** At today's $900, 32 lost trips is about **$28,800 in the first season**. Two years later you were still 15 trips (about $13,500 a year) below where you started. This cut is for three years, not one.
- **What customers say about this cut.** 41 of 70 past customers (59%) say they'll book fewer trips. Only 12 (17%) say they'll book the same.
- **Who the cut actually touches.** Charter boats land 9% of the state's summer flounder and private boats land 80%. The charter fleet is a small part of the catch, and it's the part where a fish limit turns straight into lost income.

A narrower version you could stand behind: *"The last cut cost me 19% of my trips, and I hadn't recovered two years later. Most of our customers say this one will cost us more, and it would run three years."* I'd write that version unless you can give me facts for "out of business" (see question 2). It's your call, so tell me which you want.

**Questions, most important first:**

1. **What do you want the commission to do instead?** You could ask them to reject the cut, set it at 3 instead of 2, give charter boats their own limit, or review it after one year instead of locking in three. Their staff are recommending a cut because the stock is at 78% of target. A plain "no" means arguing against their own biologists. A specific alternative gives them something they can vote for.
2. **What's your break-even?** Roughly what does a season cost you (fuel, crew, insurance, slip, boat payments), or how many trips do you need just to cover costs? If losing 30 trips puts you below that, you can honestly say this cut threatens your business. That's what would make the strong claim true.
3. **How did 2016 go for the rest of the harbor?** Did any boats close or sell after that cut? How many boats were there then compared with 11 now?
4. **Does the cut apply to private anglers too?** And would you accept some cut, or do you dispute that the stock needs one?
5. **The survey:** what did the other 17 of the 70 say? Did it ask *how many* fewer trips people would book?
6. **Anything else the commission should hear?** For example, crew you employ, or money your customers spend in town on hotels, meals and bait. Also, is there anything about you or the charter fleet the commissioners might already hold against you?

Two minutes spoken is about 260 to 280 words. Once you answer, I'll write it to that length.

On the main line: I still want it as strong as it can be, but I don't want to say anything false. Make it as strong as the facts allow.

1. We'd accept a 3-fish limit or a shorter season instead of 2 fish.
2. I don't have a break-even number to give you.
3. I don't know how the rest of the harbor did in 2016 or how many boats there were then. I only know my own books. Two other captains here have told me they'd sell if bookings drop like they did in 2016.
4. I don't know if it applies to private anglers. I don't dispute the staff's stock numbers. I have no answer to them. We'd take some cut, just not down to 2.
5. I don't know what the other 17 said or whether it asked how many fewer trips.
6. I'm Captain Ray Dunn, boat's the Sea Lark. About 70% of my trips for this season are already booked. I can give commission staff my trip logs from 2016 on. Our charter association can commit to testing a catch-reporting app with the staff next season. I don't have numbers on crew or what customers spend in town. I don't know of anything they'd hold against us.

I've made it as strong as your facts allow without saying anything false. The hardest-hitting true line is that two other captains have told you they'll sell if bookings drop like they did in 2016, so that's where the business threat goes. I left out "every boat will go out of business," since you only know your own books.

<final_document>
Good evening, Commissioners. I'm Captain Ray Dunn. I've run the charter boat Sea Lark for 22 years, one of eleven charter boats in our harbor.

I'm not here to dispute your staff's stock numbers, and we'll accept a cut. I'm asking you to make it a three-fish limit or a shorter season, not two fish.

I can tell you what the last cut did, because I keep the books. In 2016, the season after the limit was cut, my bookings fell from 170 trips to 138. That's almost one trip in five. Two years later I was back up to 155, still fifteen short. This cut would halve the limit, and it would last three years.

Our charter association asked 70 past customers about a two-fish limit. Forty-one said they'd book fewer trips. Only twelve said they'd book the same.

I run about 160 trips a season at $900 a trip. If this cut hits like the last one, that's about 30 trips and $27,000 a year off my boat, three years running. Two other captains in our harbor have told me that if bookings drop the way they did in 2016, they'll sell.

Charter boats land about 9% of this state's summer flounder. Private boats land about 80%. We're a small share of the catch, but on a charter boat the limit decides whether the trip gets booked at all.

Here's what we'll bring. I'll give your staff my trip logs from 2016 on. Our charter association will test a catch-reporting app with your staff next season. And we ask that staff weigh a three-fish limit or a shorter season before you vote on two.

Thank you.
</final_document>

A few notes:

- **Length:** It's about 290 words, which fills two minutes at a steady pace. If you run over in practice, cut the paragraph about the 9% and 80% first.
- **Your 2016 recovery is in on purpose.** You did come back to 155, and the commission could find that out. Saying it yourself, together with "still fifteen short," makes the three-year length of this cut hit harder.
- **I left out the 70% of trips already booked.** It's November, so I couldn't tell whether you meant the season just ended or next season. If those are bookings for next season, made under the four-fish limit, tell me and I'll work it in.
- **The $27,000 is your 2016 drop (19%) applied to today's 160 trips at $900.** I worded it as "if this cut hits like the last one," so it's a projection and not a prediction.
